title: Harnessing the Tides
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Every day, in most parts of the world, the sea rises and falls twice. The force behind this movement is the gravity of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun, and it is so regular that tide tables can be printed years in advance. Engineers have long been tempted by the idea of capturing that energy because, unlike wind or sunshine, the tides never fail to arrive. The difficulty has always been the price.

The oldest method is the tidal barrage, a long wall built across the mouth of an estuary. The world's first large tidal power station, on the Rance estuary in France, opened in 1966 and is still in operation. A barrage works in a series of stages. At high tide, sluice gates in the wall are opened and seawater flows into a basin behind it. The gates are then closed, trapping the water as the tide falls outside. When the difference in water level is great enough, the trapped water is released through turbines built into the barrage. The moving water spins the turbine blades, which drive a generator, and the electricity it produces is fed into the national grid.

Barrages can generate large amounts of power, but they have serious drawbacks. A wall across an estuary changes the way water, mud and sand move through it, and can damage the feeding grounds of wading birds. Fish may be injured by the turbines or blocked from reaching their spawning rivers. The construction costs are also enormous, and many projects have been cancelled before a single stone was laid. A station that opened at Sihwa Lake in South Korea in 2011 avoided some of these problems because it was built into a seawall that already existed, which kept costs down and prevented new damage.

A second approach is the tidal lagoon, a curved wall built out from the shore in shallow water. Because it encloses an area of open sea rather than blocking a river, it interferes less with the natural flow of water. Supporters say lagoons could also be used to protect coastlines from flooding. Critics reply that electricity from the first lagoon proposed in Britain would have cost more than electricity from a new nuclear plant, and in 2018 the government declined to support it.

The newest and most promising technology is the tidal stream turbine, which resembles an underwater wind turbine. Fixed to the seabed in channels where the current is strong, its blades turn as the water flows past, in both directions. Since water is roughly 800 times denser than air, a blade can be much shorter than the blade of a wind turbine and still produce the same power. A group of these machines off the north coast of Scotland has been supplying electricity since 2016.

Developers face challenges, though. Seawater corrodes metal, and storms can damage equipment that is difficult to reach for repairs. Installing a turbine in a fast channel requires specialised vessels, which can work only during the short periods when the water is almost still. Early prototypes failed because their blades were damaged by floating debris, and the companies that built them lost their investors' money. Each failure made funding harder to obtain.

Even so, many experts believe tidal power will find a place in the energy mix. Its great advantage is that it is predictable: a grid operator knows exactly when output will rise and fall and can plan around it, whereas the output of wind power has to be forecast. Costs are expected to fall as more turbines are built, as happened with solar panels and wind farms. Nobody expects the tides to supply more than a modest share of any country's electricity, but as a steady partner to other renewable sources they may prove very valuable.

items.s: The Moon is the only cause of the tides.
e: the gravity of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun

items.s: Tide tables can be produced years in advance.
e: tide tables can be printed years in advance

items.s: The power station on the Rance estuary has been closed down.
Large numbers of fish have been killed by barrage turbines.
e: Fish may be injured by the turbines
items.w: The passage says fish may be injured, but gives no figures for deaths.

items.s: The Sihwa Lake station was built into an existing structure.
e: it was built into a seawall that already existed

items.s: Tidal lagoons block the flow of rivers.
The British government supported the first proposed lagoon in 2018.
e: in 2018 the government declined to support it

items.s: Tidal stream turbines can only generate power when the tide is rising.
e: its blades turn as the water flows past, in both directions

items.s: Tidal stream turbines have been supplying electricity off Scotland since 2016.
Solar panels became cheaper more quickly than wind farms did.
e: as happened with solar panels and wind farms
items.w: The two are mentioned together; no comparison of speed is made.

items.q: According to paragraph A, what has always been the main difficulty with tidal power?
e: The difficulty has always been the price.

items.q: Why can a tidal stream turbine blade be shorter than a wind turbine blade?
o: It is made from lighter metal.
Water is much denser than air.
It is fixed to the seabed.
e: Since water is roughly 800 times denser than air

items.q: Early tidal prototypes failed mainly because
o: their blades were damaged by floating debris.
they could not be anchored to the seabed.
storms washed them away from the channel.
e: Early prototypes failed because their blades were damaged by floating debris

Fish may be unable to reach their spawning rivers.

The noise of turbines may frighten whales.
Coastal erosion may destroy nesting sites.

blocked from reaching their spawning rivers
